name: Mastoid crevasse technique

card.summary: A deep plane neck-lift step in which the platysma and SMAS tissue is anchored into a groove behind the ear at the mastoid, used by surgeons to sharpen the jawline and neck angle.
card.note: A surgical technique performed under anaesthesia by facial plastic surgeons; published data come from surgeon-authored case series.

quick.overview:
The mastoid crevasse is a surgical anchoring point used in deep plane face and neck lifts. Surgeons secure the lifted platysma and SMAS layers into a groove at the mastoid bone behind the ear, pulling tissue upward and backward. The aim is a more defined jawline and a sharper angle between jaw and neck.

Published work, mostly by the surgeons who developed it, reports that the technique deepens the measurable angle under the jaw (the gonial angle) compared with traditional suspension to the anterior mastoid. Later variants connect tissue from the hyoid bone or the SMAS flap to the same crevasse.
quick.how: It is carried out by a surgeon as part of a deep plane facelift or neck lift, under anaesthesia. The platysma and SMAS are released from their tethering ligaments, lifted along a chosen vector, and sutured into the crevasse. It is not something done outside an operating room, and patients who ask about it typically discuss it as one of several options in a consultation.
quick.risks: As with any facelift or neck lift, risks include those of surgery and anaesthesia; the available reports are surgeon-authored series with small samples and mainly female patients. The technique is discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to achieve a sharper neck angle.

lead: The mastoid crevasse technique is a step in deep plane neck lifting. It refers to a small groove or recess near the mastoid process behind the ear into which surgeons suture the platysma and SMAS layers so that tissue is held up and back, with the aim of creating a clearly defined jawline and neck angle [1][2].

In looksmaxxing, jaw and neck definition are widely discussed parts of facial appearance, and neck angle surgery is listed among the hardmaxxing procedures. The technique is a surgical route to a more defined angle beneath the jaw, as opposed to non-surgical changes such as fat reduction.

The published literature consists mainly of papers from facial plastic surgeons. A 2024 case series of 79 patients (158 hemifaces, 95 percent female) reported measured gonial depth before and after surgery, and later papers describe variants such as the bucket handle technique and a hyoid-to-mastoid crevasse neo-ligament [1][4].

chain: Platysma and SMAS released from tethering points
Tissue suspended into the mastoid crevasse
Deeper gonial angle and sharper cervicomental line
angle.text: Surgeons use the crevasse as an anchor so the lifted neck tissue pulls back and up, giving a more sculpted line along the jaw. Reported measurements show a deeper angle below the jaw after the technique than before surgery.

paras: Modern face and neck lifting releases tethering points along the superficial musculoaponeurotic system and platysma complex, so the deep tissue can glide and be repositioned [1]. Deep plane approaches build on the work of Hamra, who first described deep plane rhytidectomy, and recent advances include incision placement, handling of the SMAS-platysma complex and the mastoid crevasse [2].

In the technique, platysma and SMAS tissue is sutured into the crevasse in a chosen vector. A 2024 analysis of 71 patients (142 hemifaces, 90 percent female, mean age 57.8) measured the vectors of lifting, finding an average SMAS lift vector of 70.8 degrees, platysmal 87.0 degrees and skin 58.2 degrees, with females showing a more vertical SMAS vector than males [3].

In the 79-patient series, mean gonial depth before intervention was about 9.4 mm on the left and 8.3 mm on the right. Traditional suspension to the anterior mastoid produced about 15.8 and 13.7 mm, while after the crevasse technique the depth was about 23.2 and 22.5 mm; patients were followed for one year [1].

A 2025 report describes a bucket handle modification in which a triangle of intact SMAS extending from the mandibular angle toward the sternocleidomastoid is sutured back to the crevasse, intended to augment the gonial angle and strengthen the neck lift vector [4]. A 2026 paper introduced a hyoid-to-mastoid crevasse neo-ligament that elevates the submandibular gland, reporting improvements in cervicomental, gonial and a newly named OnderKaak angle in 25 patients [5].

Published studies are surgeon-authored series and technique reports: the 79-patient measurement series [1], the 71-patient vector analysis [3], the bucket handle technique report [4] and a 25-patient hyoid-to-mastoid study [5]. These samples were mostly female, and a 2024 chapter on deep plane anatomy gives the lead authors' view that deep plane techniques produce rejuvenation results with less need for fat grafting or implants [2].

timeline.event: Series of 79 patients measures gonial depth with the crevasse technique [1]; vector analysis of 71 patients published [3].
Hyoid-to-mastoid crevasse neo-ligament and OnderKaak angle introduced [5].
